cards.f: Arrangement and motion of particles in a solid
cards.b: Regular lattice, very close together; particles vibrate about fixed positions.

cards.f: Arrangement and motion of particles in a liquid
cards.b: Irregular, touching; particles slide past each other.

cards.f: Arrangement and motion of particles in a gas
cards.b: Random, far apart; particles move fast in random directions.
Random, jerky motion of small visible particles (e.g. smoke) in a fluid, caused by collisions with much smaller, fast-moving fluid particles.

cards.f: Gas pressure in terms of particles
cards.b: Particles colliding with the container walls; total force per unit area.

cards.f: Heating a gas at constant volume: effect on pressure
cards.b: Particles move faster, hit walls harder and more often, so pressure increases.

cards.f: Compressing a gas at constant temperature
cards.b: Particles closer together so more collisions per unit area per second; pressure increases.

cards.f: Melting and boiling point of water
Why does temperature stay constant during melting?
cards.b: Energy input is used to overcome the forces between particles, not to increase their speed.
Escape of the more energetic particles from the surface of a liquid; it cools the liquid.
Boiling: only at the boiling point, throughout the liquid (bubbles). Evaporation: any temperature, only at the surface.

cards.f: Three ways to speed up evaporation
cards.b: Higher temperature, larger surface area, air movement over the surface.
Lattice vibrations plus delocalised (mobile) electrons carrying energy; metals are the best conductors.
Heated fluid expands and becomes less dense, so it rises; cooler, denser fluid sinks to replace it.

cards.f: Best and worst surfaces for thermal radiation
cards.b: Dull black: best emitter and absorber. Shiny white/silver: worst emitter and absorber, best reflector.

short.q: Explain, in terms of particles, why a gas exerts a larger pressure when heated in a fixed-volume container.
short.model: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. They hit the walls more often and with more force, so the force per unit area increases.
points: greater force per collision / pressure increases

short.q: Explain why a vacuum flask keeps liquids hot.
short.model: The vacuum between the double walls stops conduction and convection; the silvered surfaces reduce radiation; the stopper reduces heat loss by convection.

short.q: Explain why sweating cools the body.
short.model: The more energetic particles escape from the sweat by evaporation, leaving the remaining liquid with lower average kinetic energy, so it cools.
points: remaining particles lower average kinetic energy

short.q: Describe an experiment to show that a dull black surface is a better emitter than a shiny one.
short.model: Use a Leslie cube filled with hot water. Place a detector the same distance from each face and compare readings; the dull black face gives the highest reading.

short.q: Explain how a convection current heats a room from a radiator.
short.model: Air next to the radiator is heated, expands and becomes less dense so it rises. Cooler denser air sinks to take its place, setting up a circulation.
points: warm air expands, less dense, rises
